en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics 50.
The Training Rule on Military Displays.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, while staying with an army for two or three nights, went to watch military exercises, troop reviews, battle arrays, and the inspection of the ranks.
One of those monks from the group-of-six, having gone to the military exercises, was pierced by an arrow.
People mocked that monk, saying:
“Venerable sir, was the battle well-fought? How many lakhs did you win?
Being thus ridiculed by those men, that bhikkhu became dejected.
The people criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“How can it be that the recluses, sons of the Sakyan, come to see a military review?
It is a loss for us, it is a misfortune for us, that we come to a military review for the sake of our livelihood and for the sake of our wives and children.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and carping in this way.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the bhikkhus of the group of six go to see a military review? ... [The Buddha asked:
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that you went to see a military review?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, go to see a battle?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

‘If a monk, while staying with an army for two or three nights, should go to a military review, a troop muster, a military array, or to see a regiment, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"If a bhikkhu dwells with an army for two or three nights" means:
dwelling there for two or three nights.
"A battle array" (uyyodhikaṃ) is as follows:
Where a clash is seen.
"A muster of forces" means:
so many elephants, so many horses, so many chariots, so many foot soldiers.
An array of troops (*senābyūha*) means:
"Let there be elephants here, let there be horses here, let there be chariots here, let there be infantry here.
A division (*anīka*) means...
The elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry corps.

Three elephants constitute the rear of the elephant corps; three horses constitute the rear of the cavalry; three chariots constitute the rear of the chariot corps; four men armed with swords constitute the rear of the infantry corps.
If he goes to see them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Wherever he stands and sees [them], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having left the range of sight, he sees them again and again, there is an offense of expiation.
If he goes to see each one individually, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he stands where he is and sees [the person], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, having left the range of vision, he sees again and again, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
Standing in the monastery,
he sees that after a bhikkhu has occupied a place for standing, sitting, or lying down, a scuffle is seen occurring there;
or he sees it while walking along the path.
Having gone when there is business to be done, he sees;
in times of misfortune;
for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The tenth training rule concerning military displays is finished.
The fifth section on the Naked Ascetics is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The cake, the story of Upananda,
and likewise the three attendants.
Mahānāma, Pasenadi,
Senāviḍḍha— these are the ten.
